Parlous means dangerously uncertain, precarious, or in a bad and risky state — a condition where things could easily fall apart or get much worse.

When you call something parlous, you are saying it is not just difficult — it is teetering on the edge. There is a sense of fragility to it, like a structure that could collapse at any moment. Think of it as a warning word: things are serious, unstable, and the outcome is far from safe.

Parlous is a grave word. It does not describe mild inconvenience. It describes a situation where the danger is real, the uncertainty is high, and the ground beneath you feels unsteady. It often implies that things have been getting worse over time, rather than describing a single sudden shock.

It also carries a slightly formal, literary quality — the kind of word you would find in a serious newspaper editorial, a novel, or a speech. It lends weight and seriousness to whatever it describes.

Parlous almost always describes states, conditions, situations, and times — not physical objects. You would not say "a parlous knife." You would say:

  • "The country's economy is in a parlous state." — meaning the economy is dangerously unstable and could collapse.
  • "The charity's finances are parlous." — meaning the money situation is so bad that the charity's survival is at risk.
  • "We live in parlous times." — meaning the current era is full of danger and uncertainty.
  • "Their health is in a parlous condition." — meaning their health is dangerously fragile.
  • "The negotiations are in a parlous position." — meaning the talks could break down catastrophically at any moment.

Notice the pattern: parlous state / parlous condition / parlous situation / parlous times / parlous position are the most natural and common pairings. These collocations (word partnerships) are the backbone of how this word is used in practice.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Dangerous is a broad, everyday word for anything that can cause harm. Perilous is more vivid and dramatic, often used for physical danger (a perilous mountain climb). Precarious focuses on instability — something that could tip over.

Parlous sits closest to precarious, but it adds a layer of accumulated seriousness. It usually describes a state of affairs — social, financial, political, medical — that has become deeply troubled and could worsen at any moment. It is more formal and grave than precarious, and more abstract and structural than perilous.

This is a somewhat formal and literary word, used more in written English than in casual speech. It is particularly common in British English, appearing frequently in quality journalism, political commentary, and literature. You might hear it less often in everyday American conversation.

It is not a dead word — it is still used today — but it has an old-world, slightly elevated feel to it. When a writer chooses parlous over simply saying bad or dangerous, they are deliberately signalling seriousness and depth.

There is a much older, now rarely-used sense of the word. Centuries ago, parlous also meant dangerously clever, cunning, or mischievously shrewd — used to describe a person who was too sharp for their own good, or too clever in a way that caused trouble. You might encounter this meaning in very old literature (Shakespeare, for instance, uses it this way). Today, this meaning is essentially obsolete. If you come across it in a modern text, it will almost certainly be the first meaning — precarious and dangerous.

Whenever you see or want to use parlous, ask yourself: "Is this situation serious, unstable, and in real danger of getting much worse?" If yes, parlous fits perfectly. It is the word for a state of affairs that is walking a tightrope over a very long drop.
